# Diet and chick growth

In [Lab 7](BLR_lab_chick_growth.html) we followed the same 50 chicks from hatching to day 21. We allowed chicks to have their own growth curves around a common population mean. Each chick received one diet throughout the experiment, so diet is a **chick-level covariate**.

We now ask whether the mean growth trajectory differs between diets. A difference of 20 g at day 10, for example, could persist throughout the study, or the gap could widen as the chicks grow. We first look for evidence of any association with diet. If we find one, we then ask whether the size of the difference depends on age.

# Setup and data

Save your script as `lab8.R` in your `week4` folder. The chick weights are available in R, as in Lab 7. Install the packages with `pak` if needed, as in [Lab 1](BLR_lab_center_fixed.html#install-pak-once).

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(pak)
pkg_install(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "lmerTest", "emmeans"))
```

```{r}
#| label: chick-data
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lmerTest)
library(emmeans)

chicks <- as.data.frame(datasets::ChickWeight)
```

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

# Explore the observed trajectories by diet

We can get a first impression of the diet differences by comparing chicks at the same age. At each weighing day, we calculate the mean weight of the chicks observed on each diet.

```{r}
#| label: observed-diets
diet_means <- chicks |>
  group_by(Diet, Time) |>
  summarize(observed = mean(weight), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(diet_means, aes(Time, observed, color = Diet)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = Diet), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Age (days)", y = "Observed mean weight (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Each point is one observed diet mean. The lines join successive means for the same diet. At any given age, the vertical gaps show the differences in grams between groups.

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 1"}
How similar are the four groups at hatching? How do the gaps between their mean weights change as the chicks grow?
:::

# Specify the three models

We start with the final model from Lab 7. Its random intercept and random linear slope allow chicks to differ in weight and growth rate at day 10. We keep those random effects in all three models. In the interaction model, the fixed effects let curvature differ between diets, and chicks on the same diet share that curvature.

| Model | What does it allow? |
|---|---|
| Growth alone | All four diets share one quadratic mean trajectory. |
| Add diet | Each diet can shift the mean curve up or down by a constant amount. |
| Add diet and its interactions with age | Each diet has its own intercept, linear slope, and curvature. |

The models use the same weighings and different **fixed effects**, so we fit all three by **maximum likelihood** (`REML = FALSE`). As in Lab 7, we measure age in weeks from day 10. Diet 1 is the reference. Adding `Diet` allows the other three diets to differ from Diet 1 at day 10. The two interaction terms allow those differences to change with age.

```{r}
#| label: fit-diets
chicks$week_c <- (chicks$Time - 10) / 7
model_growth_ml <- lmer(weight ~ week_c + I(week_c^2) +
                          (1 + week_c | Chick),
                        data = chicks, REML = FALSE)
model_diet_ml <- update(model_growth_ml, . ~ . + Diet)
model_interaction_ml <- update(model_diet_ml,
                               . ~ . + Diet:week_c + Diet:I(week_c^2))
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 2"}
Which two models would you compare to test for **any association with diet**? If you find evidence of an association, which comparison tells you whether the weight differences change with age?
:::

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

# Test the overall association with diet

When we pass two nested models fitted with `lmer()` to `anova()`, R performs a **likelihood-ratio test (LRT)**. Here the models are nested because setting the nine diet coefficients in `model_interaction_ml` to zero gives `model_growth_ml`.

Pass the two fitted models to `anova()`, writing the simpler model first. The test asks whether allowing each diet to have its own mean growth curve improves the fit more than we would expect if all four diets shared one curve.

```{r}
#| label: overall-diet-test
anova(model_growth_ml, model_interaction_ml)
```

Read the second row. `Chisq` is twice the gain in log likelihood, `Df` counts the added coefficients, and `Pr(>Chisq)` gives the p-value for testing those coefficients together.

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 3"}
What evidence does the test give for an association between diet and mean weight?
:::

# Test whether diet differences change with age

If there is little evidence of an overall association, we can stop with the common mean trajectory. If there is evidence of an association, we use the same test with a different starting model. This time the simpler model, `model_diet_ml`, already allows a constant weight difference between diets. Testing the added diet-by-age interactions together tells us whether those differences change as the chicks grow.

```{r}
#| label: age-diet-test
anova(model_diet_ml, model_interaction_ml)
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 4"}
What evidence does the test give that differences in mean weight between diets change with age?
:::

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

# Estimate mean weights at selected ages

To see how large the diet differences are, we return to the scale of the original weighings. We use REML for the selected interaction model and estimate the mean weight on each diet at hatching, day 10, and day 21. As in Lab 6, `at` tells `emmeans()` which values we want. The ages enter the model as `(days - 10) / 7`, and `I(week_c^2)` evaluates the quadratic term at each of those same ages.

```{r}
#| label: estimated-diet-means
model_diet <- update(model_interaction_ml, REML = TRUE)
days <- c(0, 10, 21)
weight_means <- emmeans(model_diet, ~ Diet | week_c,
                        at = list(week_c = (days - 10) / 7),
                        lmer.df = "satterthwaite")
weight_means
```

The four rows for `week_c = 0` give the estimated mean weights and 95% confidence intervals on day 10. To plot the table, use the `emmean` column for weight and convert `week_c` back to days with `10 + 7 * week_c`.

```{r}
#| label: fitted-diet-means
diet_means_plot <- as.data.frame(weight_means)
diet_means_plot$Time <- 10 + 7 * diet_means_plot$week_c

ggplot(diet_means_plot, aes(Time, emmean, color = Diet)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = Diet), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = days) +
  labs(x = "Age (days)", y = "Estimated mean weight (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Each point shows one estimated mean from the table. The straight lines connect the three selected ages for each diet.

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 5"}
How does the ordering of Diets 3 and 4 by estimated mean weight change from day 10 to day 21?
:::

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

# Compare diets at day 21

Use `pairs()` to compare the estimated mean weights you just plotted. With four diets there are six pairs at each age. The Bonferroni correction adjusts the p-values for those six comparisons separately at each age.

```{r}
#| label: pairwise-diets
pairs(weight_means, adjust = "bonferroni")
```

Day 21 is 11 days after the reference age, so read the block labeled `week_c = 1.57` (11/7 weeks). In each row, `estimate` is the first diet’s estimated mean weight minus the second’s, in grams. Compare the adjusted `p.value` with 0.05.

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 6"}
At day 21, which pairs of diets differ significantly in estimated mean weight after the Bonferroni correction?
:::
